warmup.q: List.of(1) and List.of(1, 2, 3) both return a List<Integer>. What do you expect getClass() to say for each?
options: Both are the same private immutable class
Two different private classes, chosen by the factory from the number of elements
List itself, since List.of is defined on the interface
warmup.why: List.of is a static factory, so it can return any implementation it likes. In JDK 21 it returns List12 for one or two elements and ListN for more, both private classes. A constructor could never do that: new X() always gives you an X. An interface can't be instantiated, so List itself is impossible.

sections.h: Static factory methods are constructors with names
sections.html:
A static factory method is a static method that returns an instance of its class, or of some class behind an interface. Effective Java opens with it (item 1: consider static factory methods instead of constructors), and the JDK is full of them: List.of, Duration.ofMinutes, Integer.valueOf, HttpClient.newHttpClient, Thread.ofVirtual.

A constructor can do one thing: make a new object of exactly that class. A static factory can do four things a constructor can't.

  1. It has a name. Duration.ofMinutes(2) and Duration.ofSeconds(2) both take a long. Two constructors with the same parameter types can't exist, and new Duration(2) would say nothing anyway.
  2. It can return a cached instance. Integer.valueOf(100) hands back the same object every time.
  3. It can return any subtype, chosen from the input. List.of(1) and List.of(1, 2, 3) return two different private classes. EnumSet.noneOf picks a set backed by a single long when the enum has 64 constants or fewer, and a larger one otherwise. Callers never see the class names.
  4. The class it returns doesn't have to exist when the factory is written. DriverManager.getConnection(url) returns a Connection from whichever JDBC driver on the classpath accepts the URL, found through ServiceLoader. The Oracle driver in your service was written long after java.sql.

The downsides are small. A class with only private constructors can't be subclassed, which pushes you toward composition and costs little. Factories are also harder to spot in an IDE than constructors, so stick to the usual names: of, from, valueOf, parse, newX, create.

For your own value types, make this the default. Make the constructor private and offer Money.ofMinor(1250, "EUR") and Money.parse("12.50 EUR"). With the constructor private, every Money in the system went through your validation.

try.title: Watch the JDK's factories choose
steps: Read FactoriesInTheJdk. For each of the first four lines, predict the class name you'll see. The Kotlin twin adds three lines for Kotlin's own listOf.
Run it with the command below.
Try EnumSet.noneOf(TimeUnit.class).getClass() in your IDE's auto-complete: can you type RegularEnumSet yourself?

code.title: FactoriesInTheJdk.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l02; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.EnumSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Static factories in the JDK pick the class for you. Predict each class name before you run this. */ public class FactoriesInTheJdk { public static void main(String[] args) { // the factory picks an implementation based on the input System.out.println("List.of(1) -> " + List.of(1).getClass().getSimpleName()); System.out.println("List.of(1, 2, 3) -> " + List.of(1, 2, 3).getClass().getSimpleName()); System.out.println("EnumSet of TimeUnit -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(TimeUnit.class).getClass().getSimpleName() + " (" + TimeUnit.values().length + " constants)"); System.out.println("EnumSet of scripts -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(Character.UnicodeScript.class).getClass().getSimpleName() + " (" + Character.UnicodeScript.values().length + " constants)"); // the factory can hand back a cached instance instead of a new one System.out.println("valueOf(100) twice -> same object? " + (Integer.valueOf(100) == Integer.valueOf(100))); System.out.println("Duration.ofSeconds(0) -> same as ZERO? " + (Duration.ofSeconds(0) == Duration.ZERO)); // and its name says what you get, which a constructor can't System.out.println("Duration.ofMinutes(2) -> " + Duration.ofMinutes(2)); } }

alt.title: FactoriesInTheJdk.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l02 import java.time.Duration import java.util.EnumSet import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit // The same JDK factories called from Kotlin, plus Kotlin's own. Predict each class name first. fun main() { // JDK static factories pick an implementation from the input println("List.of(1) -> " + java.util.List.of(1).javaClass.simpleName) println("List.of(1, 2, 3) -> " + java.util.List.of(1, 2, 3).javaClass.simpleName) println("EnumSet of TimeUnit -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(TimeUnit::class.java).javaClass.simpleName + " (" + TimeUnit.entries.size + " constants)") println("EnumSet of scripts -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(Character.UnicodeScript::class.java).javaClass.simpleName + " (" + Character.UnicodeScript.entries.size + " constants)") // Kotlin's factory functions do the same (full names, since two of these are nested classes) println("listOf() -> " + listOf<Int>().javaClass.name) println("listOf(1) -> " + listOf(1).javaClass.name) println("listOf(1, 2, 3) -> " + listOf(1, 2, 3).javaClass.name) // a factory can hand back a cached instance, and its name says what you get println("Currency EUR twice -> same object? " + (java.util.Currency.getInstance("EUR") === java.util.Currency.getInstance("EUR"))) println("Duration.ofMinutes(2) -> " + Duration.ofMinutes(2)) }

try.expect: List12 for one element and ListN for three. RegularEnumSet for TimeUnit (7 constants) and JumboEnumSet for Character.UnicodeScript (well over 64 constants). Both same object? lines print true, because the factories handed back cached instances. None of these classes are public, so you can't name them in your code. The factory is the only door. Kotlin's listOf plays the same game: EmptyList, Collections$SingletonList and Arrays$ArrayList, depending on how many elements you pass.

sections.h: Factory Method: let someone else choose the class
sections.html:
The GoF Factory Method is a related idea with a confusingly similar name. A class needs to create something, but it shouldn't decide which concrete class. In the book's version, an abstract creator declares a creation hook and subclasses override it:

Java
abstract class CheckoutService {
    protected abstract PaymentGateway createGateway();       // the factory method
    final String pay(long amountMinor, String token) {
        return createGateway().charge(amountMinor, token);
    }
}
class AdyenCheckout extends CheckoutService {
    protected PaymentGateway createGateway() { return new AdyenGateway(); }
}
Kotlin
abstract class CheckoutService {
    protected abstract fun createGateway(): PaymentGateway      // the factory method
    fun pay(amountMinor: Long, token: String) = createGateway().charge(amountMinor, token)
}
class AdyenCheckout : CheckoutService() {
    override fun createGateway(): PaymentGateway = AdyenGateway()
}

That is one subclass per product, just to pick a constructor. Since Java 8, a function does the same job. A Supplier<PaymentGateway> (in Kotlin, a () -> PaymentGateway) is a factory, and a constructor reference is the shortest way to write one:

Java
record Checkout(Supplier<? extends PaymentGateway> gateways) {
    String pay(long amountMinor, String token) { return gateways.get().charge(amountMinor, token); }
}
new Checkout(AdyenGateway::new);   // production
new Checkout(FakeGateway::new);    // test
Kotlin
class Checkout(private val gateways: () -> PaymentGateway) {
    fun pay(amountMinor: Long, token: String) = gateways().charge(amountMinor, token)
}
Checkout(::AdyenGateway)   // production
Checkout(::FakeGateway)    // test

When the choice depends on data (a config value, a tenant, the BIN of a card), put it in one static factory over a sealed product family:

Java
static PaymentGateway of(Provider p) {
    return switch (p) {            // no default branch, on purpose
        case ADYEN -> new AdyenGateway();
        case STRIPE -> new StripeGateway();
        case FAKE -> new FakeGateway();
    };
}
Kotlin
fun gatewayOf(p: Provider): PaymentGateway = when (p) {   // no else branch, on purpose
    Provider.ADYEN -> AdyenGateway()
    Provider.STRIPE -> StripeGateway()
    Provider.FAKE -> FakeGateway()
}

Leave out default (or else in Kotlin). When someone adds KLARNA to the enum, this switch stops compiling, and the compiler points at the one place that needs a new gateway. With a catch-all branch that returns FakeGateway, the build stays green and real Klarna payments go to the fake. It is the factory bug I see most often in review.

People mix up the two names, so keep them apart. A static factory is about how one class hands out its own instances. Factory Method is about who decides the concrete class: not the code that uses the object.

You already write factory methods in your services under another name. A Quarkus @Produces method or a Spring @Bean method is a factory method that the container calls. It decides how to build the KafkaProducer or the issuer client, and the rest of the code injects only the interface. The container calls it when it creates the bean, not once per request, so a choice that depends on the current request (which network this card belongs to) still needs a factory you call yourself.

try.title: Break a factory on purpose
steps: Add KLARNA to the Provider enum and run it again. Read the compiler error.
Now add a catch-all as the last branch (default -> new FakeGateway(); in Java, else -> FakeGateway() in Kotlin), keep KLARNA, and run again. Where does Klarna's charge go?

code.title: GatewayFactory.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l02; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** A factory method over a sealed family, and the same factory passed around as a function. */ public class GatewayFactory { enum Provider { ADYEN, STRIPE, FAKE } sealed interface PaymentGateway permits AdyenGateway, StripeGateway, FakeGateway { String charge(long amountMinor, String token); // the static factory: an exhaustive switch over the enum, with no default branch static PaymentGateway of(Provider p) { return switch (p) { case ADYEN -> new AdyenGateway(); case STRIPE -> new StripeGateway(); case FAKE -> new FakeGateway(); }; } } record AdyenGateway() implements PaymentGateway { public String charge(long amountMinor, String token) { return "adyen:" + token + ":" + amountMinor; } } record StripeGateway() implements PaymentGateway { public String charge(long amountMinor, String token) { return "stripe:" + token + ":" + amountMinor; } } record FakeGateway() implements PaymentGateway { public String charge(long amountMinor, String token) { return "fake:ok"; } } // the modern "factory method": the caller hands in how to make the product record Checkout(Supplier<? extends PaymentGateway> gateways) { String pay(long amountMinor, String token) { return gateways.get().charge(amountMinor, token); } } public static void main(String[] args) { for (Provider p : Provider.values()) { System.out.println(p + " -> " + PaymentGateway.of(p).charge(1_250, "tok_42")); } System.out.println("test checkout -> " + new Checkout(FakeGateway::new).pay(1_250, "tok_42")); } }

alt.title: GatewayFactory.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l02 // A factory over a sealed family, and the same factory passed around as a function. enum class Provider { ADYEN, STRIPE, FAKE } sealed interface PaymentGateway { fun charge(amountMinor: Long, token: String): String companion object { // the factory: an exhaustive when over the enum, with no else branch fun of(p: Provider): PaymentGateway = when (p) { Provider.ADYEN -> AdyenGateway() Provider.STRIPE -> StripeGateway() Provider.FAKE -> FakeGateway() } } } class AdyenGateway : PaymentGateway { override fun charge(amountMinor: Long, token: String) = "adyen:$token:$amountMinor" } class StripeGateway : PaymentGateway { override fun charge(amountMinor: Long, token: String) = "stripe:$token:$amountMinor" } class FakeGateway : PaymentGateway { override fun charge(amountMinor: Long, token: String) = "fake:ok" } // the modern "factory method": the caller hands in how to make the product class GatewayCheckout(private val gateways: () -> PaymentGateway) { fun pay(amountMinor: Long, token: String) = gateways().charge(amountMinor, token) } fun main() { for (p in Provider.entries) { println("$p -> ${PaymentGateway.of(p).charge(1_250, "tok_42")}") } println("test checkout -> ${GatewayCheckout(::FakeGateway).pay(1_250, "tok_42")}") }

try.expect: The first run prints one charge per provider and test checkout -> fake:ok. With KLARNA added, the build fails, pointing at the factory: javac says error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values, and kotlinc says 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'KLARNA' branch or an 'else' branch. With a catch-all branch it compiles and prints KLARNA -> fake:ok: a customer's payment would go to the fake gateway, and nothing warns you.

sections.h: Kotlin factories: companion, invoke and sealed results
sections.html:
Kotlin has no static, so its factories live in three other places.

The companion object is the direct translation of a Java static factory. Make the constructor private and put the factory next to it:

Java
public final class Card {
    private final Network network;
    private final String last4;
    private Card(Network network, String last4) { this.network = network; this.last4 = last4; }

    public static CardResult parse(String raw) { /* validate, then new Card(network, last4) */ }
}
Kotlin
class Card private constructor(val network: Network, val last4: String) {
    companion object {
        fun parse(raw: String): CardResult { /* validate, then Card(network, last4) */ }
    }
}

An operator fun invoke on the companion lets callers write what looks like a constructor call, Fee(290), while you run a factory that validates or returns a cached instance. Use it sparingly: readers expect Fee(290) to make a new object.

The third shape is a top-level function named like the type. The Kotlin coding conventions allow a factory function to share the name of the abstract type it returns, and kotlinx.coroutines does exactly that: Job(), CoroutineScope(context) and MutableStateFlow(0) are functions that return a private implementation class.

What a factory returns matters as much as where it lives. A parser that throws makes every caller remember a try. A factory that returns a sealed result makes the compiler remember for them:

Java
public sealed interface CardResult {
    record Valid(Card card) implements CardResult {}
    record Invalid(String reason) implements CardResult {}
}

switch (Card.parse(input)) {             // no default
    case CardResult.Valid v -> charge(v.card());
    case CardResult.Invalid i -> reject(i.reason());
}
Kotlin
sealed interface CardResult {
    data class Valid(val card: Card) : CardResult
    data class Invalid(val reason: String) : CardResult
}

when (val r = Card.parse(input)) {      // no else
    is CardResult.Valid -> charge(r.card)
    is CardResult.Invalid -> reject(r.reason)
}

Add a third case later, say Expired, and every when without an else stops compiling until it handles it. Java 21 gives you the same check with a sealed interface, records and a switch with type patterns, as the Java twin shows. Throw exceptions for bugs and broken infrastructure. Return a sealed result for outcomes the caller is expected to handle, like a mistyped card number.

try.title: Let the compiler find the missing case
steps: Run CompanionFactories (Kotlin, or its Java twin) with the command below and read the three parse lines.
Add a fourth result: data class Blocked(val country: String) : IbanResult in Kotlin, or record Blocked(String country) implements IbanResult {} in Java. Predict what happens, then run.
Fix it by adding a branch for Blocked to describe, not an else or default.

code.title: CompanionFactories.kt
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l02 // Three Kotlin factory shapes, and a factory that returns a sealed result instead of throwing. class Iban private constructor(val country: String, val digits: String) { override fun toString() = "$country****${digits.takeLast(4)}" companion object { // 1. a named factory in the companion: Iban.parse("...") fun parse(raw: String): IbanResult { val s = raw.replace(" ", "").uppercase() return when { s.length < 15 -> IbanResult.TooShort(s.length) !s.take(2).all(Char::isLetter) -> IbanResult.BadCountry(s.take(2)) else -> IbanResult.Ok(Iban(s.take(2), s.drop(2))) } } } } sealed interface IbanResult { data class Ok(val iban: Iban) : IbanResult data class TooShort(val length: Int) : IbanResult data class BadCountry(val prefix: String) : IbanResult } class Fee private constructor(val bps: Int) { override fun toString() = "Fee($bps bps)" companion object { private val standard = Fee(290) // 2. operator invoke: callers write Fee(290) and get the cached instance operator fun invoke(bps: Int): Fee = if (bps == 290) standard else Fee(bps) } } interface Ledger { fun post(entry: String) } // 3. a top-level function named like the interface, as kotlinx.coroutines does with Job() and CoroutineScope() fun Ledger(): Ledger = object : Ledger { override fun post(entry: String) = println(" ledger <- $entry") } fun describe(r: IbanResult): String = when (r) { // no else: the compiler checks every case is here is IbanResult.Ok -> "ok: ${r.iban}" is IbanResult.TooShort -> "too short (${r.length} chars)" is IbanResult.BadCountry -> "bad country code '${r.prefix}'" } fun main() { listOf("DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 00", "DE89 3704", "12345678901234567890").forEach { println("parse(\"$it\") -> ${describe(Iban.parse(it))}") } println("Fee(290) === Fee(290)? ${Fee(290) === Fee(290)}") println("Fee(150) === Fee(150)? ${Fee(150) === Fee(150)}") Ledger().post("fee 29.00 EUR") }

alt.title: CompanionFactoriesJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l02; import java.util.List; /** The Java twin of CompanionFactories.kt: static factories, a cached instance, and a sealed result. */ public class CompanionFactoriesJava { static final class Iban { final String country, digits; private Iban(String country, String digits) { this.country = country; this.digits = digits; } @Override public String toString() { return country + "****" + digits.substring(digits.length() - 4); } // 1. a named static factory: Iban.parse("...") static IbanResult parse(String raw) { String s = raw.replace(" ", "").toUpperCase(); if (s.length() < 15) return new TooShort(s.length()); if (!Character.isLetter(s.charAt(0)) || !Character.isLetter(s.charAt(1))) return new BadCountry(s.substring(0, 2)); return new Ok(new Iban(s.substring(0, 2), s.substring(2))); } } sealed interface IbanResult {} // permitted subtypes: the records in this file record Ok(Iban iban) implements IbanResult {} record TooShort(int length) implements IbanResult {} record BadCountry(String prefix) implements IbanResult {} static final class Fee { private static final Fee STANDARD = new Fee(290); final int bps; private Fee(int bps) { this.bps = bps; } // 2. Java has no operator invoke, so the cached-instance factory needs a name static Fee of(int bps) { return bps == 290 ? STANDARD : new Fee(bps); } } interface Ledger { void post(String entry); // 3. a static factory on the interface returns a hidden implementation static Ledger create() { return entry -> System.out.println(" ledger <- " + entry); } } static String describe(IbanResult r) { return switch (r) { // no default: the compiler checks every case is here case Ok ok -> "ok: " + ok.iban(); case TooShort t -> "too short (" + t.length() + " chars)"; case BadCountry b -> "bad country code '" + b.prefix() + "'"; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { for (String raw : List.of("DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 00", "DE89 3704", "12345678901234567890")) { System.out.println("parse(\"" + raw + "\") -> " + describe(Iban.parse(raw))); } System.out.println("Fee.of(290) == Fee.of(290)? " + (Fee.of(290) == Fee.of(290))); System.out.println("Fee.of(150) == Fee.of(150)? " + (Fee.of(150) == Fee.of(150))); Ledger.create().post("fee 29.00 EUR"); } }

try.expect: The first run prints ok: DE****3000, too short (8 chars) and bad country code '12', then true for the cached Fee with 290 bps and false for 150. Java has no operator invoke, so its twin needs a named factory, Fee.of(290). After adding Blocked, the build stops: kotlinc says 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Blocked' branch or an 'else' branch., and javac says the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. The compiler found the one place that needs the new case.

sections.h: Abstract Factory: one choice for a whole family
sections.html:
Sometimes you create several objects that must match. A card network gives you an authorization API and a refund API, and a Visa auth code means nothing to Mastercard's refund endpoint. If every call site picks its own authorizer and its own refunder, sooner or later a code path that runs once a month pairs a Visa authorizer with a Mastercard refunder.

Abstract Factory puts that choice in one place. One interface creates every product of the family, with one implementation per family:

Java
public interface CardNetworkClients {
    Network network();
    Authorizer authorizer();
    Refunder refunder();

    static CardNetworkClients sandbox(Network network) {
        return switch (network) {
            case VISA -> new SandboxClients(Network.VISA, "https://sandbox.visa.example", "V");
            case MASTERCARD -> new SandboxClients(Network.MASTERCARD, "https://sandbox.mastercard.example", "M");
        };
    }
}
Kotlin
interface CardNetworkClients {
    val network: Network
    fun authorizer(): Authorizer
    fun refunder(): Refunder

    companion object {
        fun sandbox(network: Network): CardNetworkClients = when (network) {
            Network.VISA -> SandboxClients(Network.VISA, "https://sandbox.visa.example", "V")
            Network.MASTERCARD -> SandboxClients(Network.MASTERCARD, "https://sandbox.mastercard.example", "M")
        }
    }
}

Callers ask for the family once, clientsFor(card.network), and take both products from it. They can't mix families because they never pick a product directly.

Each family here is one class built from settings, not a VisaAuthorizer plus a VisaRefunder. When the products are single-method interfaces, a family is just a class (or a Java record) of functions. The GoF diagram with two parallel class hierarchies is the worst case, not a requirement.

The weakness runs the other way. Adding a family is cheap: one more implementation. Adding a product, say a Tokenizer, changes the interface and every family. And with a DI container you may not need to write the factory at all: Quarkus build profiles or Spring profiles can pick the Kafka messaging family in production and an in-memory one in tests. Write the factory yourself when the choice depends on runtime data, such as the card in this request.

figure.caption: Checkout asks for a family once. Both products come from that family, so a Visa auth code never reaches a Mastercard refund.

analogy: A static factory is the counter at a bank branch. You ask for "a debit card for this account", and the clerk decides which card stock, which network and which design you get. You never walk into the print room. An abstract factory is a branch that only issues matching sets: your card, PIN letter and online-banking token all come from the same issuer, so they work together. The analogy breaks on cost: a bank can add a new kind of card at one counter, but adding a new product to an abstract factory means teaching every family to make it.
world: Card BIN routing is a factory: the first digits pick the network, and the network picks the issuer client, its base URL, its timeouts and its error mapping. Put that decision in one when over a sealed Network, return a sealed result for numbers you can't route, and inject the family factory as a function into your Quarkus resource or Temporal activity. Then a test passes a lambda that returns a fake family and records which network was asked for. For Kafka, a family of producer plus consumer plus serde, chosen once by a build profile, keeps the in-memory test setup from leaking into production config.
mistake: The most common mistake is a factory switch or when with a default or else branch that returns something plausible, such as a fake or the most common implementation. It looks defensive. In practice it turns "you forgot to handle the new provider" from a compile error into a production incident. Write the switch over a sealed type or an enum with no default, so the compiler forces a decision for every new case. If some input really has no product, return a sealed Invalid result instead of guessing.

compare.title: A validating factory that returns a sealed result

java.title: Money.java
java.html: public final class Money { private final long minor; private final String currency; private Money(long minor, String currency) { this.minor = minor; this.currency = currency; } public static Money ofMinor(long minor, String currency) { // named and validating if (minor < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount"); return new Money(minor, currency); } public sealed interface Parsed permits Ok, Bad {} public record Ok(Money money) implements Parsed {} public record Bad(String reason) implements Parsed {} public static Parsed parse(String text) { // "12.50 EUR" String[] parts = text.trim().split(" "); if (parts.length != 2) return new Bad("expected '<amount> <currency>'"); try { long minor = new BigDecimal(parts[0]).movePointRight(2).longValueExact(); return new Ok(ofMinor(minor, parts[1])); } catch (ArithmeticException | IllegalArgumentException e) { return new Bad("not an amount: " + parts[0]); } } } // caller: the compiler checks both cases are handled String shown = switch (Money.parse(input)) { case Money.Ok(Money m) -> "charge " + m; case Money.Bad(String why) -> "rejected: " + why; };

kotlin.title: Money.kt
kotlin.html: class Money private constructor(val minor: Long, val currency: String) { companion object { @JvmStatic fun ofMinor(minor: Long, currency: String): Money { require(minor >= 0) { "negative amount" } return Money(minor, currency) } @JvmStatic fun parse(text: String): Parsed { // "12.50 EUR" val parts = text.trim().split(" ") if (parts.size != 2) return Parsed.Bad("expected '<amount> <currency>'") val minor = parts[0].toBigDecimalOrNull() ?.movePointRight(2) ?.runCatching { longValueExact() }?.getOrNull() ?: return Parsed.Bad("not an amount: ${parts[0]}") return if (minor < 0) Parsed.Bad("negative amount") else Parsed.Ok(Money(minor, parts[1])) } } } sealed interface Parsed { data class Ok(val money: Money) : Parsed data class Bad(val reason: String) : Parsed } // caller val shown = when (val p = Money.parse(input)) { is Parsed.Ok -> "charge ${p.money}" is Parsed.Bad -> "rejected: ${p.reason}" }

compare.note: The shape is the same: private constructor, named factories, a sealed result and an exhaustive switch or when at the call site. Java 21 deconstructs the result with record patterns (case Money.Ok(Money m)), Kotlin smart-casts it after is. The real difference is where the factory lives. Kotlin has no static: ofMinor is a method on the companion object, so Java callers would write Money.Companion.ofMinor(...) without @JvmStatic. Kotlin also gives you operator fun invoke and top-level factory functions, and its named arguments remove a lot of the constructor ambiguity that pushes Java code toward factories in the first place.

worked.title: Replace ambiguous constructors with named factories

steps.say: A Refund class grew four constructors. Look at the last line and decide what it creates before reading on.
steps.code: public class Refund { public Refund(String paymentId, long amountMinor) { ... } // partial public Refund(String paymentId) { ... } // full public Refund(String paymentId, long amountMinor, String reason) { ... } // partial, with reason public Refund(String paymentId, String reason) { ... } // full, with reason } new Refund("p-1", "duplicate"); // ?

alt.html: class Refund { constructor(paymentId: String, amountMinor: Long) { ... } // partial constructor(paymentId: String) { ... } // full constructor(paymentId: String, amountMinor: Long, reason: String) { ... } // partial, with reason constructor(paymentId: String, reason: String) { ... } // full, with reason } Refund("p-1", "duplicate") // ?

steps.say: It's a full refund with a reason, but only the parameter types say so. Adding a chargeback reversal would mean a fifth constructor with another type mix. Give each kind a name, validate there, and make the constructor private so every Refund goes through a factory.
steps.code: public final class Refund { private final String paymentId; private final OptionalLong amountMinor; // empty = full refund private final String reason; private Refund(String paymentId, OptionalLong amountMinor, String reason) { this.paymentId = paymentId; this.amountMinor = amountMinor; this.reason = reason; } public static Refund full(String paymentId, String reason) { // 1. the name says what you get return new Refund(paymentId, OptionalLong.empty(), reason); } public static Refund partial(String paymentId, long amountMinor, String reason) { if (amountMinor <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("partial refund needs a positive amount"); // 2. validate per kind return new Refund(paymentId, OptionalLong.of(amountMinor), reason); } } Refund.full("p-1", "duplicate"); Refund.partial("p-1", 500, "damaged item");

alt.html: class Refund private constructor( val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long?, // null = full refund val reason: String, ) { companion object { fun full(paymentId: String, reason: String) = Refund(paymentId, null, reason) // 1. the name says what you get fun partial(paymentId: String, amountMinor: Long, reason: String): Refund { require(amountMinor > 0) { "partial refund needs a positive amount" } // 2. validate per kind return Refund(paymentId, amountMinor, reason) } } } Refund.full("p-1", "duplicate") Refund.partial("p-1", 500, "damaged item")

steps.say: Downstream, a full refund also releases the authorization hold. When the kinds behave differently, let the same factories return different records (or data classes) behind a sealed interface. Callers don't change, and code that handles refunds can switch over the two cases with the compiler checking it covers both. In Kotlin, @JvmStatic keeps Refund.full(...) working for Java callers, and Kotlin callers could also write Refund.Partial(paymentId = "p-1", amountMinor = 500, reason = "damaged"): named arguments already remove the ambiguity that started this.
steps.code: public sealed interface Refund permits FullRefund, PartialRefund { String paymentId(); static Refund full(String paymentId, String reason) { return new FullRefund(paymentId, reason); } static Refund partial(String paymentId, long amountMinor, String reason) { return new PartialRefund(paymentId, amountMinor, reason); // 3. the factory picks the record } } record FullRefund(String paymentId, String reason) implements Refund {} record PartialRefund(String paymentId, long amountMinor, String reason) implements Refund { PartialRefund { // 4. the invariant lives in the record if (amountMinor <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive"); } }

alt.html: sealed interface Refund { val paymentId: String data class Full(override val paymentId: String, val reason: String) : Refund data class Partial(override val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long, val reason: String) : Refund { init { require(amountMinor > 0) { "amount must be positive" } } // 4. the invariant lives in the class } companion object { @JvmStatic fun full(paymentId: String, reason: String): Refund = Full(paymentId, reason) @JvmStatic fun partial(paymentId: String, amountMinor: Long, reason: String): Refund = Partial(paymentId, amountMinor, reason) // 3. the factory picks the class } }

lab.title: A card factory, a network family, and a checkout that only knows interfaces
steps: Run the tests. All nine fail with NotImplementedError.
Write Card.parse in Card.kt. Apply the four checks from its KDoc in order and return CardResult.Invalid(reason) with the exact reason strings. Only parse may call the private constructor.

Write CardNetworkClients.sandbox. One private class built from settings (network, base URL, prefix) can serve both families. Use require for the cross-network checks, and an exhaustive when with no else.
Write Checkout.pay as a when over Card.parse(rawPan). Call clientsFor only for a valid card.
Run the tests until all nine pass.
hints: raw.replace(" ", ""), then digits.all { it in '0'..'9' } and digits.length !in 12..19 cover the first two checks. luhnOk is already written.
For the network, digits.startsWith("4") is Visa. For Mastercard, check digits.take(2).toInt() in 51..55 || digits.take(4).toInt() in 2221..2720.
Authorizer and Refunder are fun interfaces, so Authorizer { card, amount -> ... } builds one from a lambda.
require(condition) { "message" } throws IllegalArgumentException when the condition is false.

drill.title: A sealed-result factory from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. In Kotlin (or Java, with a static parse), write Email with a private constructor and a companion parse(raw: String): EmailResult. It returns Ok(email) when the trimmed text has exactly one @ with something on both sides, and Invalid(reason) otherwise. Then write a caller that uses when (or switch) with no else or default.

answer.html: class Email private constructor(val value: String) { companion object { fun parse(raw: String): EmailResult { val parts = raw.trim().split("@") return if (parts.size == 2 && parts.all { it.isNotEmpty() }) EmailResult.Ok(Email(raw.trim())) else EmailResult.Invalid("expected name@domain") } } } sealed interface EmailResult { data class Ok(val email: Email) : EmailResult data class Invalid(val reason: String) : EmailResult } fun receiptTarget(raw: String): String = when (val r = Email.parse(raw)) { is EmailResult.Ok -> "sending receipt to ${r.email.value}" is EmailResult.Invalid -> "skipped: ${r.reason}" }

alt.title: Java
alt.html: public final class Email { private final String value; private Email(String value) { this.value = value; } public String value() { return value; } public static EmailResult parse(String raw) { String[] parts = raw.trim().split("@", -1); return parts.length == 2 && !parts[0].isEmpty() && !parts[1].isEmpty() ? new EmailResult.Ok(new Email(raw.trim())) : new EmailResult.Invalid("expected name@domain"); } } public sealed interface EmailResult { record Ok(Email email) implements EmailResult {} record Invalid(String reason) implements EmailResult {} } static String receiptTarget(String raw) { return switch (Email.parse(raw)) { case EmailResult.Ok ok -> "sending receipt to " + ok.email().value(); case EmailResult.Invalid bad -> "skipped: " + bad.reason(); }; }

recap: A static factory is a constructor with a name. It can cache, return any subtype, and pick the class from its input (List.of, EnumSet.noneOf, DriverManager.getConnection).
Make the constructor private and validate in the factory, so every instance in the system is a valid one.
The GoF Factory Method (a subclass overrides a creation hook) is now usually a Supplier<T> or () -> T, often a constructor reference such as FakeGateway::new.
A factory's switch or when over a sealed type or enum gets no default or else, so a new case is a compile error at the one place that must change.

Kotlin factories live in the companion object, in operator fun invoke, or in a top-level function named like the type (Job(), MutableStateFlow(0)). Return a sealed result for outcomes callers must handle.
Abstract Factory makes a family of matching products from one choice. New families are cheap; a new product touches every family.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why CardNetworkClients.sandbox(network) has no else branch, and why Checkout takes a (Network) -> CardNetworkClients instead of calling sandbox directly.
explain.answer: With no else, the when has to name every Network. When someone adds AMEX, the factory stops compiling until they decide which family Amex gets, instead of quietly falling into a default. The function parameter keeps Checkout ignorant of which families exist and how they're built. Production passes CardNetworkClients::sandbox or a live factory, and a test passes a lambda that returns a fake family and records which network was asked for. So the choice of concrete classes lives in one place, and the checkout logic can be tested without any network client.

deeper.html:
DriverManager is a factory whose products did not exist when it was written. On first use it asks ServiceLoader for every java.sql.Driver that a JAR on the classpath lists in a META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver file. getConnection(url) then offers the URL to each driver until one accepts it. You can build the same plug-in mechanism yourself: define an interface, list the implementations in META-INF/services/<interface name>, and call ServiceLoader.load(YourInterface.class). The module system adds provides ... with ... and uses ... declarations for the same thing.

Effective Java lists conventional factory names, and sticking to them makes factories easy to find: from for a one-argument conversion (Date.from(instant)), of for aggregation (EnumSet.of(...)), valueOf, getInstance or instance, create or newInstance when each call returns a new object, getType and newType when the factory lives in another class (Files.newBufferedReader), and a bare type (Collections.list).

From Java, a Kotlin companion factory is Money.Companion.parse(...). Annotate it with @JvmStatic and Java callers can write Money.parse(...). If a Java team consumes your Kotlin library, do it for every public factory. The same goes for @JvmOverloads on functions with default arguments, which you'll meet in Builder and Prototype (lesson 3 of this track).
